title: Tongues and colors
hookLine: the diversity of your languages and colors is among His signs (30:22)

cards: Stand in the courtyard of the Great Mosque in Mecca at any hour, and listen. Indonesian, Urdu, Turkish, Hausa, Bosnian, Malay, Bengali, Somali, French, English, Arabic in a dozen accents.
Faces of every shade, from every continent, walking the same circle, many in the same white cloth. Some pilgrims come home talking less about the buildings than about the crowd.
The verse right after yesterday's has a word for what they saw.

teach.h: LANGUAGES AND COLORS BESIDE THE SKY.
teach.b: Pickthall: "And of His signs is the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the difference of your languages and colours. Lo! herein indeed are portents for men of knowledge." Look at the company the verse keeps.
The heavens, the earth, and in the same breath, the fact that people speak differently and look different. Human variety sits on the same shelf as the sky.
Not a problem to solve, and not a ranking: a sign, an aya, the same word used for a verse of the Qur'an. Who is meant to read this sign?

teach.h: A SIGN FOR THOSE WHO KNOW.
teach.b: Men of knowledge, in Pickthall's English; in Arabic, al-'alimin, those who know. As if the more you learn about people, the more there is to see.

teach.h: NATIONS AND TRIBES, TO KNOW ONE ANOTHER.
teach.b: Surah Al-Hujurat says something close: We made you nations and tribes so that you might know one another, and the noblest of you with God is the most mindful of Him.

teach.h: NO ARAB OVER NON-ARAB, EXCEPT BY TAQWA.
teach.b: And in his farewell pilgrimage sermon, reported in the Musnad of Imam Ahmad, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ said an Arab has no superiority over a non-Arab, nor a non-Arab over an Arab, nor a light-skinned person over a dark-skinned one, nor the reverse, except by taqwa.
His first community already looked like that: Bilal from Abyssinia, Salman from Persia, Suhayb, called the Roman.

This week ran from Al-Qasas through Al-'Ankabut to Ar-Rum: al-amin, do good as good was done, faith is tested, al-'ankabut, within a few years, love and mercy between. And today, the widest: difference is a sign.

how: Muslims often cite 30:22, 49:13 and the Prophet's farewell sermon to teach that no language, people or color is above another, and that only taqwa distinguishes people before God.

o: a prayer said for travelers in Mecca
a sign, and also the word for a verse
a call to gather for the pilgrimage

games.q: tongues and colors — tap the pairs.
p: a sign, and a verse of the Qur'an
nations and tribes, to know one another

s: the verse treats different languages as a curse to overcome
it counts them among God's signs, beside the heavens and earth.
the farewell sermon says no color is superior except by taqwa
reported in the Musnad of Imam Ahmad.
the first Muslim community was all from one people
it included Bilal from Abyssinia, Salman from Persia, and Suhayb the Roman.

games.q: you're on Hajj, surrounded by a crowd whose languages you don't speak. the verse calls this a sign. for whom?
o: for those who know: the more you learn, the more you see.
for nobody; it's just a crowd.
games.why: 30:22: herein indeed are portents for those who know, al-'alimin.

practice: Think of someone you see often whose first language isn't yours: a neighbor, a colleague, the person at the corner shop, a classmate's parent.
Wonder for a moment what they speak at home, and how they'd say hello or thank you in it. If you pray, you can thank God for one person whose difference has taught you something.

wordCard.voice: Aya. A sign, the same word used for a verse of the Qur'an: what Ar-Rum calls the variety of human languages and colors, beside the heavens and the earth. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: your tongues and your colors, from 30:22; alsina is literally tongues.

carryVoice: Your line: difference is a sign. Variety is something to read, not to rank. That's the week.

sources.q: And of His signs is the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the difference of your languages and colours. Lo! herein indeed are portents for men of knowledge.

sources.ref: Musnad Ahmad 23489 (the farewell sermon: no Arab over non-Arab)
